title: A poet tells the life
hookLine: a poet retells the Buddha's life as a Sanskrit epic, and year three begins inside it

lines: THE SAME LIFE, A NEW VOICE.
cards: Same prince, same road, a new voice.

In year one this path walked through the Buddha's life the plain way: a dream, a grove, four sights on a road, a ride out at midnight, short scenes mostly from the old discourses and the commentaries.

Then came a whole year of his own words. Now the life comes back as a poem. Not a monk's report: a poet's, with long descriptions, speeches, gardens, gods leaning in from the sky, and a father who can't stop worrying.
For the next stretch of days, i'll read it with you, one scene at a time.

teach.h: BUDDHACARITA: THE LIFE OF THE BUDDHA.
teach.b: The poem is the Buddhacarita: the life, or the acts, of the Buddha. Tradition names its poet Ashvaghosha, and calls him a monk who was also a master of Sanskrit verse. This path follows an English translation by E.
B. Cowell. So what changes when a life becomes a poem?
A discourse might give the prince's comfort in a sentence; the poem lingers, so you hear the music in the palace and smell the gardens.

Second, people speak. The king argues, a friend makes his case for pleasure, a charioteer pleads, and the prince answers each of them in his own words. You hear the arguments he had to get past, not only the result.
Third, the sky takes part. Gods arrange what the prince sees. Doors open on their own.
Some readers take these as wonders that happened. Others read them as a poet's way of saying the whole world was turning toward this moment. The poem doesn't stop to settle it.
And fourth, it's still the same story: the dream, the birth, the sage, the sights, the leaving.
It doesn't invent a new Buddha. It slows the old one down so you can walk beside him. Not new facts: the same steps, taken slowly, one canto at a time.

how: Buddhists come to the Buddha's life through many tellings, from the discourses and commentaries to later poems like the Buddhacarita, and in some communities these stories are read aloud, studied in classes or told at festivals.

s: the poem invents a new story of the Buddha
it keeps the familiar beats: the dream, the birth, the sage, the sights, the leaving.
in the poem, people make speeches and the prince answers
the king, a friend and a charioteer all speak, and he replies to each.
the poem stops to explain whether its wonders really happened
it tells them and moves on; some readers take them as events, others as a poet's picture.

games.q: you're a poet handed the Buddha's life, a story everyone already knows. what do you do with it?
o: change the ending so it surprises people.
slow it down and let the people in it speak.
cut it to a single page.
games.why: the poem keeps the story and slows it down: gardens, music, arguments, and the prince's own answers.

practice: The poem begins with a city, the old home of a sage named Kapila, a king of the Shakya clan named Shuddhodana, and his queen, Maya.
Hold the three in mind, a city, a king, a queen, the way you'd hold the first page of a long book before anything has happened. No need to guess what comes next; just stay with the opening.
